text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard defended on Monday his plan to make some young people work for their unemployment benefits.
The country expected the government to try new ideas, Howard said, responding to opposition criticism that the scheme was just a stunt to keep some young people off the streets.
"We still have eight-and-a-half percent unemployment," Howard said. "We still have 100,000 young people out of work."
The Liberal-National government, which replaced a 13-year-old Labor administration last year, inherited unemployment above eight percent and creeping higher.

Australia has experienced generally rising unemployment since the mid-1970s. The business cycle takes the rate up and down but each peak tends to be higher than the previous peak and each trough higher than the previous trough.
"They (Australians) understand we can't fix it overnight but what they do expect and require of us is that we try different strategems," Howard said.
The government is aiming its scheme at regions where youth joblessness is high. The hours of community work will equate to the unemployment benefit paid at the usual youth wage rate.
Both sides of Australian politics say the long-term solution to unemployment is to improve the efficiency of the economy so it can grow fast enough to generate jobs.
But the two sides differ about short-term measures.
The former Labor government focussed on training people who had been out of work for more than a year.
Labor's A$1 billion-a-year programme, which was not budgeted beyond mid-1998, was sold as a way of improving the availability of trained workers, easing inflationary pressures as unemployment fell.
The Liberal-Nationals last year replaced that programme with a much cheaper boost to apprenticeships.
The opposition, calling plan to make youth work for their social security a Mickey Mouse scheme, said the government had got itself into the mess by cutting the old programmes.

"And now when they find themselves with the logical consequences -- rising youth unemployment, rising long-term unemployment -- they come in with Mickey Mouse," Opposition Leader Kim Beazley told reporters.
Unemployment was 8.6 percent in Decmeber and the goverment is forecasting little change in the first half of 1997.
The rate fell from a late-1992 peak of 11.0 percent but stopped falling at 8.4 percent in 1995.
